title: How To Implement AIOps: A 7-Step Rollout Plan (2026)
summary: Learn how to implement AIOps with Struct's 7-step plan — from observability to automated remediation. Start your AIOps rollout today.
body_markdown:
*Written by: Nimesh Chakravarthi, Co-founder & CTO, Struct*


## Key Takeaways


- Start with one measurable problem and establish a clear baseline before any tooling changes.
- Build a vendor-neutral observability foundation using OpenTelemetry and normalize all events into a shared schema.
- Sequence correlation and anomaly detection before introducing ML-driven investigation or automated remediation.
- Adopt an autonomy ladder with explicit policy gates so remediation only expands after correlation quality is proven.
- The rollout culminates in an investigation, correlation, and verification layer that closes the loop on Steps 4–7.


[Automate your on-call runbook](https://cal.com/deepanm/struct-demo)


## What Are The Four Key Stages Of AIOps?


According to[Fortinet](https://www.fortinet.com/resources/cyberglossary/aiops-future-of-it-operations) , the four key stages of AIOps are raw data collection, data aggregation, data analysis, and remediation, though other sources describe the stages somewhat differently (for example, data ingestion, correlation and anomaly detection, root-cause analysis, and automated remediation). The seven-step plan maps onto these stages directly. Steps 1–3 cover data ingestion and schema readiness. Step 4 covers correlation and anomaly detection. Step 5 covers LLM-assisted investigation. Steps 6–7 cover remediation and closed-loop verification.


[Enterprise-grade AIOps platforms deliver six core capabilities](https://alicelabs.ai/en/insights/ai-for-it-operations) : anomaly detection, event correlation, noise reduction, root cause analysis, predictive alerting, and automated remediation. Each capability operates at a reactive, proactive, or autonomous maturity level. Teams that skip the ingestion and correlation stages and jump straight to remediation consistently underperform, because[Gartner predicts organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects not backed by AI-ready data](https://xcubelabs.com/blog/aiops-implementation-roadmap) .


## What Is The 10/20-70 Rule For AI?


[BCG’s 10/20/70 rule](https://www.bcg.com/featured-insights/the-leaders-guide-to-transforming-with-ai) states that a company should allocate roughly 10% of AI effort to algorithms, 20% to technology and data, and 70% to people and processes. Applied to AIOps, the model you pick becomes the smallest decision you make. Telemetry quality and on-call workflow redesign drive the outcome.


For pilot scoping, this rule has a direct implication.[Organizations that skip the AIOps data readiness audit consistently report poor model performance in the first 90 days and incorrectly attribute this to the AI platform rather than the underlying data problem](https://alicelabs.ai/en/insights/ai-for-it-operations) . Steps 1–3 of this plan exist entirely to address the 20% before touching the 10%. That work begins with a single, measurable problem.


## Step 1: Pick One Measurable Problem And Define Success In Operational Terms


Start by baselining alert volume, MTTD, and MTTR for one service over a defined measurement window. That baseline is what makes a scoped AIOps pilot, typically 6 to 10 weeks on a single domain, produce a measurable before-and-after on mean time to resolution and alert volume[(source)](https://xcubelabs.com/blog/aiops-implementation-roadmap) . Without it, ROI claims remain qualitative.


Artifact — a one-line baseline statement:


> *Service: checkout-api | Metric: MTTR | Baseline: 38 minutes | Window: 2026-08-01 to 2026-08-31 | Alert volume: 214 pages*


You know this step worked when you can state the before number without estimating.[N-iX’s July 2026 AIOps implementation guide recommends a minimum 90-day measurement window](https://n-ix.com/aiops-implementation) . For a lean Series A–C team, a 30-day window on one high-traffic service is sufficient to establish a credible baseline before the pilot begins.


## Step 2: Build The Observability Foundation With OpenTelemetry


Instrument metrics, logs, traces, and events with[OpenTelemetry’s logs signal](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs) and[metrics signal](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics) , and route everything through a Collector.[OpenTelemetry’s documentation notes that the first step in adopting OpenTelemetry frequently involves deploying a Collector as a general-purpose logging agent](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs) . Enforce a` service.name` convention across every service before proceeding.


Artifact — a minimal Collector pipeline config:


> receivers: \[otlp, filelog\]
> processors: \[batch, resource/add_service_name\]
> exporters: \[otlp/backend, logging\]
> service.name enforced via resource processor on every pipeline


[OpenTelemetry log records carry TraceId, SpanId, Timestamp, SeverityNumber, Body, Resource, and Attributes](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs) , which are the fields that make cross-signal correlation possible.[When an application activates an OpenTelemetry SDK, it automatically correlates existing logs with any active trace and span by wrapping the log body with their IDs](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs) .


You know this step worked when one trace ID resolves across logs and metrics for a single request.[61.5% of cloud-native enterprises are actively adopting or standardizing on OpenTelemetry instrumentation](https://voxbooster.com/blog/observability-apm-statistics-2026) , which makes it a low-friction foundation for everything that follows.


## Step 3: Normalize And Enrich Events With A Concrete Schema


Map every source onto one event contract before attempting correlation.[Even two sources using the same log format can disagree on field names, so a shared format does not guarantee a shared schema](https://motadata.com/it-glossary/log-normalization) . Parsing and normalization remain distinct sequential steps. Parsing breaks a raw log line into fields. Normalization maps those fields onto a common schema.


Artifact — a normalized event JSON schema:


> {
> “timestamp”: “ISO 8601 UTC”,
> “service”: “checkout-api”,
> “environment”: “production”,
> “severity”: “critical”,
> “severity_id”: 6,
> “deployment”: “sha:abc123 | version:2.4.1”,
> “owner”: “payments-team”,
> “dependency”: \[“postgres-primary”, “stripe-api”\],
> “runbook”: “https://runbooks.internal/checkout-api/db-timeout”,
> “trace_id”: “4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736”,
> “source_system”: “datadog”
> }


A canonical event model should distinguish three timestamps: occurred_at, observed_at, and ingested_at, which makes detection delay and pipeline delay measurable. You know this step worked when a single query returns the same field names regardless of whether the source is Datadog, Sentry, or CloudWatch.


## Step 4: Start With AI-Assisted Alert Correlation


Reduce alert noise by deduplicating by fingerprint, grouping temporally, then grouping topologically using the service dependency graph.[Alert correlation attacks volume along three axes: deduplication (collapsing identical repeating alerts by fingerprint), temporal grouping (clustering alerts firing inside a sliding time window), and topological grouping (using the service dependency graph to suppress downstream symptom alerts and surface the upstream root cause)](https://iotdigitaltwinplm.com/aiops-incident-response-architecture-agentic-sre-2026) . Implement them in that order, with topology last because it requires a live, accurate dependency graph derived from OpenTelemetry spans.


Consider a before-and-after narrative. A single database connection pool saturation event in the pricing service produces alerts across four downstream services and generates a dozen distinct alert types in Datadog, Sentry, and CloudWatch simultaneously. An on-call engineer spends 30–45 minutes manually correlating across five tools before any fix begins. After correlation, one incident surfaces: *“Pricing service degraded — likely root cause, 3 downstream services affected, blast radius = checkout flow.”* This is the kind of correlation that Struct automates.


[Struct correlates Sentry issues with Datadog metrics, cloud infrastructure, GitHub deploy history, logs, traces, and other tools to produce a root-cause hypothesis](https://struct.ai/blog/struct-vs-sentry-seer) .[Struct automatically investigates every alert with intelligent auto-deduping and posts results to Slack](https://struct.ai/blog/struct-vs-sentry-seer) .


You know this step worked when one incident surfaces instead of a dozen alerts.[Organizations implementing AIOps routinely see daily alerts drop from over 5,000 to roughly 100 actionable items](https://devops.com/the-end-of-alert-fatigue-how-ai-powered-observability-is-transforming-sre-teams-in-2026) .


[See how Struct correlates alerts across your stack](https://cal.com/deepanm/struct-demo)


## Step 5: Add An LLM Investigation Layer On Structured Data


Ground the model in the normalized schema and your runbooks. Ground the model in a structured event schema with ownership, dependency, and runbook fields. Without that structure, the LLM will produce hallucinated hypotheses instead of cited, verifiable ones.[Every hypothesis must cite evidence the human can verify in one click, confidence scores must be calibrated against historical accuracy, and the system must be willing to say “I don’t know — escalating.”](https://iotdigitaltwinplm.com/aiops-incident-response-architecture-agentic-sre-2026)


Instrument the AI layer itself using[OpenTelemetry’s GenAI observability guidance](https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2026/genai-observability) . The` gen_ai.*` namespace standardizes model calls, token usage, and tool invocations across any backend.


Artifact —` gen_ai.*` spans on the investigation agent:


> invoke_agent \[root span\]
> chat gpt-4o \[gen_ai.usage.input_tokens: 1240, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens: 312\]
> execute_tool fetch_runbook \[gen_ai.tool.name: “checkout-api/db-timeout”\]
> execute_tool query_logs \[gen_ai.tool.name: “cloudwatch_query”\]


[OpenTelemetry GenAI metrics enable teams to estimate per-request cost, catch token-hungry prompts before they hit production, detect latency regressions, and monitor usage patterns across models and agents](https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2026/genai-observability) . You know this step worked when every hypothesis cites evidence a human can verify in one click, and the investigation agent’s own behavior is observable in the same pipeline as the rest of your stack. For a deeper treatment of LLM prompting and triage patterns, see How To Use Generative AI For AIOps SRE Incident Management.


## Step 6: Automate Remediation With An Autonomy Ladder And A Policy Engine


Publish the autonomy ladder explicitly and gate each level with written promotion criteria.[Autonomy is anchored to action risk rather than granted to the system as a whole](https://iotdigitaltwinplm.com/aiops-incident-response-architecture-agentic-sre-2026) . Restarting a single crashlooping stateless pod might reach L3 quickly because it is reversible and low blast radius. Failing over the primary database may never leave L2.


The five-level ladder:


1. **Monitoring:** System surfaces correlated incident only. Audit log of what was surfaced.
2. **Explain:** Adds RCA hypotheses and suggested fix. Confidence shown, evidence cited, no write access.
3. **Recommend:** Proposes a specific pre-staged runbook action. Human approves before execution.
4. **Human-Approved Auto-Execute:** Executes low-risk reversible actions after one-click approval. Policy-as-code allowlist, canary scope, auto health check, auto rollback.
5. **Bounded Auto-Execute:** Executes a bounded class of actions end to end. Strict blast-radius math, rate limits, and a kill switch on top of all prior guardrails.


Artifact — policy logic that must pass before execution:


> IF confidence_score >= 0.85
> AND blast_radius_affected_services <= 2
> AND action IN policy_allowlist
> AND environment != “production-primary”
> AND rollback_available == true
> THEN execute in canary scope
> ELSE escalate_to_human()


[If a remediation fires more than N times in M minutes, halt and page a human](https://augmentcode.com/guides/incident-response-automation) . This guardrail exists because blast radius failures at machine speed occur when a remediation that is safe for one instance executes simultaneously across a correlated fleet. For the same reason,[every automated action should carry an audit trail and a human approval gate for anything outside pre-approved scope](https://xcubelabs.com/blog/aiops-implementation-roadmap) . You know this step worked when every automated action has an audit trail and a revert path.


## Step 7: Incident Resolution Verification And Outcome Measurement


Incident resolution verification means automatically confirming an incident is actually resolved by checking live observability data, instead of only closing a ticket.[Ticket closure rate measures volume, not quality](https://operatex.dev/blog/incident-closure-rate-vs-recurrence-rate) . It rewards teams for silencing symptoms instead of eliminating root causes. A pod restart or traffic shift that returns a service to baseline does not constitute a fix.


Artifact — a verification loop:


1. Remediation executes.
2. System re-checks the original signal (error rate, latency, saturation) against the pre-incident baseline.
3. If the signal returns to baseline and holds for a stability window (for example, 5 minutes), the incident is marked resolved.
4. If the signal does not hold, the incident is automatically reopened and escalated.
5. Recurrence rate is tracked alongside MTTR as a co-equal metric.


Struct’s[Incident Tracker](https://www.producthunt.com/products/struct-2) runs a roughly 1-minute automated verification loop against observability data to confirm an incident is actually resolved. This pattern expresses incident resolution verification in production.[Verification must be performed by an actor independent of the fix proposer: if the same bot that proposes a fix also verifies it, the organization has a conflict of interest](https://operatex.dev/blog/incident-closure-rate-vs-recurrence-rate) .


You know this step worked when reopen rate falls and recurrence rate is tracked alongside MTTR.[When AIOps is genuinely working, it does more than move faster. It makes incidents smaller, recovery safer, and ownership clearer.](https://nhimg.org/faq/how-do-organisations-know-if-aiops-automation-is-actually-working)


## How To Implement AIOps In AWS


With the full plan in place, the next challenge is applying it in specific environments, starting with AWS. On AWS, use CloudWatch for metrics and logs, follow the[AWS Well-Architected operational excellence pillar](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/operational-excellence-pillar/welcome.html) for operational readiness guidance, and standardize collection with OpenTelemetry Collectors deployed as sidecars or DaemonSets. The normalized event schema and correlation steps from Steps 3–4 stay the same. CloudWatch log groups become one more source mapped onto the shared schema. AWS-specific fields such as` aws.region` ,` aws.account_id` , and` aws.ecs.cluster` slot into the schema’s` dependency` and` environment` fields. Struct integrates directly with AWS CloudWatch alongside Datadog, Sentry, GCP Logs, and Azure Logs, so the investigation layer requires no AWS-specific reconfiguration.


## What Are The Benefits Of Implementing AIOps?


The seven-step rollout produces measurable operational gains. The proof points below show what teams typically see after completing the plan:


- **Alert Volume Reduction:**[Teams previously handling over 800 alerts per day are down to 20–50 actionable items](https://devops.com/the-end-of-alert-fatigue-how-ai-powered-observability-is-transforming-sre-teams-in-2026) .
- **Lower MTTD:**[Teams deploying AIOps typically see MTTD reductions of 50 to 70 percent within the first six months](https://n-ix.com/aiops-implementation) .
- **Lower MTTR:**[Arcana reduced average developer time per investigation from 30 minutes to 2 minutes](https://struct.ai/case-study/arcana) . Struct[reports an 80%+ reduction in triage time](https://www.producthunt.com/products/struct-2) .
- **Engineer-Hours Reclaimed:**[Arcana reclaims 56 engineer-hours per month and runs 2,100+ automated investigations monthly](https://struct.ai/case-study/arcana) .
- **SLA Protection:** A Series A fintech with 40 engineers cut triage time by 80% and protected strict SLAs. The team integrated Struct in under 10 minutes.
- **Investigation Quality:** Struct’s automated investigation helpful rate is 85–90%+, meaning the vast majority of investigations provide the correct root cause and actionable next steps.


## AIOps Vs MLOps And AIOps Vs DevOps


AIOps and MLOps are frequently conflated but address different problems. AIOps applies machine learning to production operations, including alert correlation, anomaly detection, root-cause analysis, and automated remediation. MLOps is the practice of shipping, versioning, monitoring, and maintaining machine learning models in production. An AIOps platform may use MLOps practices internally to keep its own models current, but the two disciplines serve different audiences. AIOps serves on-call engineers. MLOps serves data science and ML engineering teams.[McKinsey’s State of AI survey identifies MLOps as one of the competencies organizations most commonly lack when scaling AI](https://n-ix.com/aiops-implementation) , which is a gap separate from AIOps readiness.


AIOps augments DevOps practice rather than replacing it. DevOps defines the cultural and process framework for continuous delivery and operational ownership. AIOps adds an intelligence layer on top of the observability stack that DevOps teams already operate. The CI/CD pipeline, infrastructure-as-code, and blameless postmortem culture that DevOps establishes are prerequisites for AIOps to function well, particularly the deployment metadata that makes correlation between a deploy event and a failure onset possible. Once those prerequisites are in place, the next challenge is measuring whether the AIOps program is actually working.


## Measuring AIOps: Baselines, Cadence, And Refinement


Baseline before each step, not just at the start of the program.[AIOps programs should be tracked with core operational metrics including MTTD, MTTR, alert volume per incident, percent auto-resolved without a human in the loop, and operator hours saved from manual triage](https://moveworks.com/us/en/resources/blog/build-aiops-strategy-metrics-tools-phases) . Review weekly on operational metrics and monthly on scorecards.


The recommended cadence:


- **Weekly:** Alert volume, MTTD, MTTR by incident type, on-call interruptions per week, automated resolution rate.
- **Monthly:** Recurrence rate, reopen rate, verified-fix ratio, engineer-hours reclaimed, SLA compliance.
- **Quarterly:** Decide whether to continue, adjust, or expand the program. Connect operational metrics to business objectives.[Broader business measures such as cost per ticket trends and engineering capacity for strategic projects](https://moveworks.com/us/en/resources/blog/enterprise-aiops-governance-strategy-guide-for-it-leaders) belong in the quarterly review.


The percentage of automated actions that required rollback or human override serves as a direct signal of whether autonomy is safe to expand. Treat this ratio as a promotion gate for each action class on the autonomy ladder.


## Common AIOps Implementation Pitfalls


- **Bad Telemetry Killing AIOps.**[70–80% of AIOps implementations fail to meet expectations primarily due to poor data quality and inconsistent telemetry](https://byteiota.com/aiops-2026-73-of-enterprises-ditch-reactive-monitoring) . Fix: complete Steps 1–3 before evaluating any AI capability.
- **Skipping The Data Audit.** As noted earlier, Gartner predicts organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects not backed by AI-ready data. Fix: treat telemetry readiness as a hard prerequisite, not a parallel workstream.
- **Overcomplicating The First Pilot.** Piloting everywhere instead of one domain is a named failure mode. Fix: one service, one metric, one measurement window.
- **Unclear Ownership.**[Four roles must each have a name attached for an AIOps rollout to avoid stalling: a business owner, a platform or SRE lead, a security or governance lead, and a data engineer](https://xcubelabs.com/blog/aiops-implementation-roadmap) . Fix: assign names before the pilot begins.
- **Weak Runbook Documentation.**[A mediocre model with an excellent corpus of past incidents will out-triage a frontier model reasoning from nothing](https://iotdigitaltwinplm.com/aiops-incident-response-architecture-agentic-sre-2026) . Fix: invest in runbooks before investing in model selection.
- **Insufficient Training Data For The Model.**[Historical telemetry should cover at least 90 days before deployment so ML models have enough data to establish a reliable baseline](https://n-ix.com/aiops-implementation) . Fix: run the Collector and normalize events for 90 days before enabling correlation.
- **Automating Remediation Before Correlation Quality Is Proven.**[Automated remediation should be introduced only after detection and correlation prove reliable on real production data](https://xcubelabs.com/blog/aiops-implementation-roadmap) . Fix: measure correlation false-positive rate for at least one full incident cycle before advancing to Step 6.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What Minimum Team Or Tooling Maturity Does AIOps Require?


A team needs three things before AIOps delivers reliable value: basic structured logging with trace IDs, an alerting channel (Slack, PagerDuty, or equivalent), and at least one observability tool producing metrics (Datadog, CloudWatch, Grafana, or Prometheus). Teams already using Sentry for exceptions, a cloud logging platform, and Slack for alerts are in a strong starting position. Teams with no logging, no trace IDs, and no alerting triggers will need to complete Steps 1–3 of this plan before any AI layer can function. Struct’s 10-minute setup is designed for teams already operating this baseline stack and connects to existing integrations rather than replacing them.


### How Does AIOps Work With Existing Systems And Workflows?


AIOps sits on top of existing observability tooling as an intelligence and investigation layer. It does not replace Datadog, Grafana, Sentry, or CloudWatch. The normalized event schema in Step 3 maps each source onto a shared contract, and the correlation layer in Step 4 reads from that schema. Engineers continue working in Slack, reviewing alerts in their existing tools, and merging PRs in GitHub. Struct integrates directly into Slack alerting channels and posts investigation results to the same thread where the alert fired. The workflow change for on-call engineers stays minimal. Instead of opening five tools, they open one Struct dashboard with the correlated timeline already built.


### How Long Does An AIOps Rollout Take?


A focused single-use-case AI pilot with a clean integration point and a defined evaluation harness[can ship to a production-grade MVP in 6–10 weeks](https://alicelabs.ai/en/insights/ai-consulting-rates-2026) , though pilots generally take 6–12 weeks depending on integration complexity and scope. Later steps, such as adding an investigation layer and automating remediation, extend the timeline further depending on runbook quality and the number of action classes considered for automation. Full cross-domain correlation and staged autonomy form an ongoing program rather than a fixed end date.[Early value, specifically alert volume reduction and faster triage, is typically measurable within the first 8 to 12 weeks](https://techtweekinfotech.com/aiops-implementation-roadmap) . As mentioned in Step 1, a focused pilot typically takes 6–10 weeks.


### What If Telemetry Or Documentation Is Limited?


Limited telemetry constrains what AIOps can do, yet it does not block starting. Begin with whatever structured logs and metrics exist, deploy the OpenTelemetry Collector to normalize what is available, and treat the gaps as a prioritized backlog. The normalized schema in Step 3 makes gaps visible. Fields that cannot be populated from any source become the instrumentation gaps to close first. For runbook documentation, Struct accepts custom instructions and on-call runbooks pasted directly into the platform. Even a partial runbook covering the three most frequent failure patterns is enough to ground the LLM investigation layer and produce useful hypotheses.


### How Do Security, Privacy, Access, And Compliance Work?


[Struct is SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliant (trust.struct.ai)](https://trust.struct.ai/) , which covers the compliance requirements of the vast majority of Series A–C B2B SaaS companies. Logs are accessed and processed ephemerally, and they are not warehoused by Struct. For teams with strict VPC requirements where no logs can leave the internal network, Struct’s current architecture requires access to logs via integrations (AWS, GCP, Datadog) and is not currently suited to fully on-premise deployments. On the AI instrumentation side,[OpenTelemetry’s GenAI conventions keep prompt and response content out of standard span attributes by default; content capture requires explicit opt-in](https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2026/genai-observability) and should be gated behind a redaction processor in the Collector before reaching any storage backend.


### How Do Less-Experienced Engineers Participate Safely?


The autonomy ladder in Step 6 is the primary safety mechanism for junior engineers. At L1 (Explain) and L2 (Recommend), the system provides a cited hypothesis and a proposed action. The engineer reviews and approves but does not need to derive the diagnosis from scratch. Struct acts as an automated senior engineer for the first pass, digesting company-specific runbooks to provide a heavily contextualized starting point for any alert. The same Series A fintech mentioned earlier used this pattern to safely expand on-call participation to newer engineers after integrating Struct, because every alert arrived with blast radius, root cause hypothesis, and suggested next steps already populated. The on-call engineer’s job shifts from log-hunting to hypothesis validation, which requires far less institutional knowledge.


## Where Struct Fits In An AIOps Rollout


Struct is an agentic production on-call system that executes Steps 4–7 of this plan without requiring a platform team or a multi-month deployment. It sits on top of existing observability, including Datadog, Grafana, Sentry, CloudWatch, GCP Logs, Azure, Prometheus, and Loki, as an investigation and verification layer. It does not replace any of them.
